Affect profiles.notes: The four quadrants (mad scientist, cheerleader, judge, poet) Brooks uses to classify emotional baselines by positive and negative affect intensity, measured via PANAS.

Agency.notes: The episode's organising concept — the disposition to change the world around you rather than wait for permission. Schoening: 'I don't think agency is very evenly distributed.'

Airbnb.notes: Company listed in Gil's investment/advisory background

AlexNet.notes: AI milestone discussed as an early signal of deep learning acceleration

AlphaGo / Lee Sedol.notes: DeepMind's Go-playing system and Sedol's famous loss — Schoening's example of AI exceeding the top human in a defined domain.

Andrew Mason.notes: Founder of Groupon; ousted as CEO in 2013. Source of Eric's email-frequency death-spiral anecdote.

Anduril.notes: Defense technology company discussed in relation to market/team exceptions

Anthropic.notes: AI safety lab; uses an outside Long-Term Benefit Trust of AI-safety trustees to appoint a faction of its for-profit board.

Apple.notes: Cited for parts-pairing on iPhones and for shredding traded-in devices to prevent harvest.

Arthur Brooks.notes: Harvard social scientist and bestselling author; coined the everyday vocabulary of macros, idols, and the strivers curse used throughout this conversation.

August Krogh.notes: 1920 Nobel laureate in Physiology; co-founder of Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium (predecessor to Novo Nordisk).

BlackRock.notes: World's largest asset manager; Lenny associates it with brand drift (Vital Farms anecdote, unverified).

Bob Moesta.notes: JTBD practitioner; cited as the practical voice on jobs-to-be-done.

Bob Waldinger.notes: Director of the Harvard Study of Adult Development (Grant Study); source for the seven habits of happy-and-healthy late life.

Brahma Muhurta.notes: An hour and 36 minutes before dawn — the 'Creator's time' in Vedic tradition. Brooks rises at 04:30 to train and pray inside this window.

Bret Taylor.notes: Sierra co-founder; quoted via his 'software is a garden, you need to tend to it' framing about SaaS maintenance.

Bret Victor.notes: Designer/researcher whose 'Stop Drawing Dead Fish' talk is the philosophical anchor for why Notion designers prototype in code, not Figma, for AI products.

Brian Chesky.notes: Airbnb co-founder; cited as another source for the 'world is made by people no smarter than you' idea.

Brian Lovin.notes: Notion designer Schoening calls out as a top exemplar of agency — already blurs engineering and design, recruits actively.

Bruce Ames.notes: Patrick's late mentor; cited as the rare 'cheerleader' affect profile — relentlessly positive and successful.

Build the Life You Want.notes: Brooks and Oprah Winfrey's 2023 happiness manual on managing the three macronutrients.

Carl Sagan.notes: Cited via Cosmos as the populariser of Paul MacLean's triune-brain model.

Cat Wu.notes: Head of product for Claude Code at Anthropic; mentioned for the Anthropic-runs-on-Slack anecdote.

Chris Berube.notes: Producer for 99% Invisible; reported and co-hosts this segment.

Clayton Christensen.notes: Harvard professor; originator of the jobs-to-be-done framework Schoening invokes around customer needs.

Cloudflare.notes: Network/security company; the episode treats it as a mission-emergence example for democratizing HTTPS.

CoWoS.notes: Advanced packaging capacity related to AI infrastructure constraints

Code.notes: Charles Petzold's 'Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software.' Schoening's recommendation for how computers actually work.

Coinbase.notes: Crypto company discussed as an index-like investment thesis example

Conway's law.notes: Melvin Conway's 1968 observation that software architecture mirrors the org chart of the team that built it.

Cory Doctorow.notes: Novelist, activist, journalist; coined 'enshittification' and authored the 2025 book of the same name.

Cosmos.notes: Carl Sagan's TV series and book; cited as the popular vehicle for the triune-brain framework.

Costco.notes: Membership-warehouse retailer; Eric cites it as having a governance fortress that protects margin discipline.

Creatine.notes: Basic supplement discussed in the longevity segment

Creatine monohydrate.notes: Brooks takes 10g/day; the second 5g is cited for emerging cognitive-benefit evidence.

Cyberspace.notes: William Gibson's term, invoked here for the 'cyberspace is everything, turning inside out' image — digitization spreading from screens into physical goods.

DMCA Section 1201.notes: 1998 US law making it a federal felony to break digital locks; originally aimed at MP3 piracy, now used to block third-party device repair.

Dan Gilbert.notes: Harvard psychologist whose boredom experiments showed people will self-administer electric shocks rather than sit unstimulated.

Default mode network.notes: The brain network active in mind-wandering and self-reflection; suppressed when scrolling and re-engaged when bored — Brooks's neuroscientific argument for protecting boredom.

Demos not memos.notes: The GitHub product-review mantra Schoening still applies: give people something to react to instead of writing a PRD.

Derate.notes: Tractor software intentionally reducing horsepower in response to a sensor or emissions fault; effectively a soft kill switch.

Dieter Rams.notes: Legendary industrial designer; the 'walking around a museum disapprovingly' video Schoening pinned to his X profile.

Drive it like it's stolen.notes: Schoening's mantra to himself at Notion: act with founder-like urgency even though you didn't start the company.

Dropbox.notes: Cited for its menu-bar icon as a 'tiny core' example of a single small detail being the product's superpower.

Elad Gil.notes: Guest; investor, operator, author, CEO of Gil & Co

Enshittification.notes: Cory Doctorow's three-stage platform-decay framework: serve users, lock them in, extract value.

Enshittification (book).notes: Cory Doctorow's 2025 book, 'Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse, And What to Do About It.'

Epson.notes: Named alongside HP as printer-ink lock-in example.

Eric Liu.notes: Notion PM Schoening cites as proof of agency-driven role evolution — moved from writing PRDs to building prototypes directly.

Eric Ries.notes: Author of The Lean Startup (2011) and Incorruptible (2026). Founder of the Long-Term Stock Exchange.

European Union.notes: Passed a 2024 directive requiring member-state right-to-repair laws by summer 2026.

Facebook.notes: Worked example for the three-stage enshittification cycle.

Figma.notes: Design tool whose usage is splitting at Notion — some designers move to code prototypes, others lean in. Subject of the Jevons-paradox aside.

First 10% is free.notes: The new economics of building: the first 10% of any project takes almost no effort now, but the last 10% is still the 90% that matters.

Four idols.notes: Aquinas's worldly substitutes for transcendence — money, power, pleasure, fame. Brooks: everyone is beguiled by one; naming yours is the start of freedom from it.

Frank Gehry.notes: Cited as the kind of celebrated designer whose museum pieces Rams dismantles in the pinned video.

Frederick Winslow Taylor.notes: Author of The Principles of Scientific Management (1911); the Taylorism fad Eric contrasts with Follett.

From Strength to Strength.notes: Brooks's 2022 book on designing the second half of life around four practices: jump, serve, worship, connect.

GPT-3.notes: AI milestone discussed as a transformative signal

Gay Gordon-Byrne.notes: Executive director of the Repair Association; right-to-repair advocate.

Geoffrey Litt.notes: Ink & Switch researcher who works with Schoening on the malleable-software direction at Notion.

Gil & Co.notes: Elad Gil's multi-stage investment, holding, and operating company

GitHub.notes: Where Schoening previously led design and where ~10% of pre-LLM contributions came from designers — the founding evidence for 'designers should code.'

Groupon.notes: Daily-deal company; Andrew Mason's cautionary tale of email-frequency erosion of a one-email-a-day promise.

HBM.notes: High-bandwidth memory, part of the AI compute bottleneck discussion

HP.notes: Named alongside Epson as printer-ink lock-in example.

Harvard Business School.notes: Brooks teaches 'Leadership and Happiness' to MBA students; the four-idols exercise in this episode is from his classroom.

Harvard Study of Adult Development.notes: 85-year longitudinal study (originally the Grant Study) that identified the seven habits predictive of happy, healthy old age.

HashiCorp.notes: Acquisition example in market and infrastructure software discussion

Hedonic treadmill.notes: The pattern where each achievement resets your baseline upward, so wanting always outruns having.

Hemispheric lateralization.notes: McGilchrist's framing of the right hemisphere as 'why' (meaning, love, mystery) and the left as 'how' (technique, tasks). Modern digital life over-uses the left.

Heroku.notes: PaaS company where Schoening ran design; cited as the touchstone for 'developer experience as a product.'

Iain McGilchrist.notes: Oxford psychiatrist whose hemispheric-lateralization work underwrites Brooks's claim that modern life is left-brain-only.

Ibogaine.notes: Psychoactive treatment discussed in the medicine segment

Ikigai.notes: Japanese concept of vocation at the intersection of love, skill, need, and pay; Schoening invokes it as the right way to choose what to build.

Incorruptible.notes: Eric Ries's 2026 book on governance structures that protect mission-driven companies from financial gravity.

Industrial foundation.notes: Corporate structure where a for-profit operating company is owned and governed by a nonprofit foundation; widespread in Denmark (Novo, Carlsberg) and Germany (Bosch, Zeiss).

Ink & Switch.notes: Independent research lab whose malleable-software work Schoening leans on; Geoffrey Litt is there.

Instacart.notes: Company listed in Gil's investment/advisory background

Interoperability.notes: Whether two products can work together. Parts-pairing breaks interoperability by software fiat.

Ivan Illich.notes: Philosopher; Tools for Conviviality is the intellectual lineage Schoening draws on for malleable software.

Jailbreaking.notes: Hacking around a device's software lock to install or run software the manufacturer doesn't permit.

James C. Scott.notes: Anthropologist; Seeing Like a State is one of Schoening's recommended reads.

Jared Wilson.notes: Seventh-generation Missouri farmer; named plaintiff in the John Deere right-to-repair class action.

Jevons paradox.notes: Increasing efficiency increases total usage; Schoening invokes it to predict Figma usage could rise alongside vibe coding, not fall.

Jobs to be done.notes: Clayton Christensen / Bob Moesta framework that Schoening uses as a sanity check on what customers actually want.

John Deere.notes: Agricultural-equipment maker at the center of the tractor right-to-repair fight.

Lenny Rachitsky.notes: Host of Lenny's Podcast; former Airbnb PM and author of Lenny's Newsletter.

Long-Term Benefit Trust.notes: Anthropic's governance instrument — an outside trust of AI-safety experts (without equity) that appoints a faction of the for-profit board.

Long-Term Stock Exchange.notes: SEC-registered stock exchange Eric founded; promotes long-term-focused listing standards.

Malleable software.notes: Software that works closer to the interest of its users than to the interest of the corporation that makes it. The opposite of the locked-down app model.

Marie Krogh.notes: Danish physiologist and diabetic; co-founder of the Novo Nordisk lineage. Her diabetes diagnosis drove the trip to Toronto to license insulin.

Marshmallow test.notes: Mischel's classic delayed-gratification study; Brooks uses it as a warning — strivers learn to defer marshmallows forever and never eat any.

Martin Shkreli.notes: Notorious for raising Daraprim price 5455%; Eric uses him as the archetype of pharmaceutical price-gouging the Kroghs feared.

Mary Parker Follett.notes: 1920s management theorist; rediscovered by Peter Drucker. Eric closes the episode with her 'invisible leader' concept.

Max Schoening.notes: Head of product at Notion. Previously a PM at Google, designer at Heroku, VP of Design and part-time engineer at GitHub under Nat Friedman, and a two-time founder.

Mitchell Hashimoto.notes: HashiCorp co-founder; cited for the Ghostty terminal as exemplar of taste-driven engineering.

Mother Teresa.notes: Invoked via Malcolm Muggeridge as the modern exemplar of moral beauty.

Notion.notes: Schoening's employer; the malleability-and-agency case study running through the conversation.

Novo Nordisk.notes: Danish pharma giant; owned by Novo Nordisk Foundation (industrial-foundation structure). Founded 1922 as Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium by Marie & August Krogh.

OpenAI.notes: Maker of Codex; representative of the labs-vs-real-users contrast Schoening draws.

PIRG.notes: Public Interest Research Group; estimated $3B in 2023 farm-equipment repair downtime.

Parts pairing.notes: Manufacturer locks a device's software to only accept first-party replacement parts, even when a generic part is mechanically compatible.

Paul MacLean.notes: Neuroscientist; proposed the triune-brain framework Brooks uses to separate pleasure (limbic) from enjoyment (prefrontal).

Philip Morris.notes: Tobacco giant; bought Vectura in 2021, denounced by British Thoracic Society.

Post-traumatic growth.notes: Empirical finding that >90% of people who suffer real loss or trauma report growth on the other side — provided they lower their resistance to the pain.

Public Benefit Corporation.notes: U.S. corporate form (especially in Delaware) requiring directors to balance profit with stated public benefits. Eric's two-page protective filing.

Quibi.notes: Short-form video startup that famously failed; Eric uses it as an example of a 'Lean Startup is dead' backlash that didn't pan out.

Repair Association.notes: Industry-and-advocacy group led by Gay Gordon-Byrne pushing right-to-repair legislation.

Reverse bucket list.notes: Write down your worldly attachments and cross them out — 'easy come, easy go' — to disarm the wants that drive the hedonic treadmill.

Rhonda Patrick.notes: Host of FoundMyFitness; biomedical scientist focused on aging, nutrition, and longevity.

Right to repair.notes: The movement (and growing body of US state and EU law) requiring manufacturers to enable owner and third-party repair.

SSRIs.notes: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; effective at reducing ventrolateral-prefrontal-cortex rumination but most useful when paired with cognitive-behavioral practice.

SaaSpocalypse.notes: The argument that AI will collapse the SaaS industry as users build their own tools. Schoening's take: greatly exaggerated — people still want maintenance and specialists.

Seeing Like a State.notes: James C. Scott. Schoening's other recommended read on what gets lost when we standardize and centralize.

Shareholder primacy.notes: Doctrine (popularized post-1970 by Milton Friedman) that boards' fiduciary duty is to maximize shareholder returns; Eric calls this a recent 40-year-old invention sold as natural law.

Simon Baron-Cohen.notes: Cambridge psychologist on autism and hemispheric lateralization; cited for the developmental side of right- vs left-brain dominance.

Simon Last.notes: Notion engineer whose maxim 'every manual intervention in agent-written code is a bug' Schoening cites as the engineering bar.

SpaceX.notes: Hard-tech example used in market-entry and disruption discussion

Stripe.notes: Payments company discussed as a growth and venture example

Striver's curse.notes: Brooks's term for working toward a goal because the limbic system lies that arrival will feel permanent — then the dopamine drop when you arrive sends you chasing the next thing.

The Good Life.notes: Bob Waldinger's book summarising the Harvard Grant Study findings on the predictors of happy old age.

The Lean Startup.notes: Eric Ries's foundational 2011 book on MVPs, build-measure-learn, and validated learning.

The Meaning of Your Life.notes: Brooks's 2026 book on the modern meaning crisis and the neuroscience of finding purpose.

Thomas Aquinas.notes: Catholic theologian; identified the four worldly idols Brooks uses with his MBA students.

Three macronutrients of happiness.notes: Enjoyment, satisfaction, and meaning. The central framing of the episode; you need all three in balance, like protein, carbs, and fat.

Tim Cook.notes: Apple CEO, quoted from his 2019 investor letter warning that repair (rather than replacement) is Apple's biggest revenue risk.

Tim Ferriss.notes: Host of The Tim Ferriss Show

Tiny core.notes: Schoening's framing: every great product has one tiny detail that is the superpower (iPhone multitouch, GitHub pull request, Notion blocks, Dropbox menu-bar icon).

Tools for Conviviality.notes: Ivan Illich, 1973. The philosophical case for tools that users can shape themselves — Schoening's recommended read on malleable software.

Triune brain.notes: MacLean's three-layer model (reptilian / limbic / prefrontal). Brooks uses it to argue pleasure is limbic and enjoyment is prefrontal.

Tyler Cowen.notes: Economist; Marginal Revolution; cited for the idea that society is not capped by intelligence.

Vanta.notes: Sponsor of this episode; SOC 2 / compliance automation.

Vectura Group.notes: UK inhaler-therapeutics company (asthma/COPD), University of Bath spin-out. Acquired by Philip Morris in 2021 for £1.1bn over board objections — the cautionary tale.

Vibe coding.notes: Building software conversationally with LLMs without traditional engineering rigor. Schoening: the amount of software has gone up; the quality has not.

Vital Farms.notes: Pasture-raised egg brand; Lenny's example of perceived quality erosion under new ownership (anecdotal).

Whole Foods.notes: Natural-foods grocer acquired by Amazon; recurring example of post-acquisition mission drift.

William Gibson.notes: Cited for coining 'cyberspace' and the line 'cyberspace is everything, so turning inside out.'

WorkOS.notes: Sponsor of this episode; enterprise-readiness APIs (SSO, SCIM, RBAC).

Zeiss.notes: German optics company; one of the oldest industrial-foundation companies, structured in 1885 by Ernst Abbe under the Carl Zeiss Stiftung.
